# Writing the piece

Before you write, ask the user for what you are missing. The user's request is never everything the user knows. Send one message with at most six questions, the most useful first. Ask only what would change the piece and what the request does not already answer. Look for these:

- **What the reader gets and what it costs them.** The terms as they touch this reader: pay, price, dates, what they keep, what they lose, what they can still do if they change their mind.
- **What answers the reader's main objection.** Name the objection this reader will raise and ask what the user has that answers it: what has already been done or offered about it, what has changed since, what the proposal leaves in place.
- **What shows the writer can deliver, or knows the reader's world.** A record, a credential, a time they did this before, someone who has checked their work or will vouch for it.
- **What the writer can commit to.** A date, a number, a named person, what happens if it is missed.
- **The reader.** Who exactly reads this, what they already think of the writer, and anything they hold against the writer, when the request does not say.
- **The names and dates the piece cannot go out without.** Who it is addressed to, who signs it, a deadline.
- **What the reader will find out anyway.** Close with one open question: is there a cost, a limit, a weak number or a past failure that the request leaves out and this reader knows or will learn?

When the answers come back, write the piece as you normally would, and hand it over. When the user does not know something, write without it and do not guess.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter can say.

1. **What's the "a third will close within a year" figure based on?** Nothing in your list supports it yet. Nine closures in two years, with no known cause, doesn't point to a third of all independents closing in twelve months. The plan and both newspapers will ask where the number came from, and one claim that falls apart can take the rest of the letter down with it. Do you have something behind it? For example: how many independents there are in the state in total, a survey, or a count of your 38 owners who've said they can't keep going at these rates. If not, I'd use a figure you can stand behind, such as "X of the 38 of us say we cannot continue past [date]." Is there such a number?

2. **What exactly do you want the plan to do, and by when?** For example: a minimum payment of acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee written into the July 1 PBM contract, payment rates the PBM has to disclose, or a meeting before a certain date. The letter needs one clear ask.

3. **Have you already raised this with the plan or the PBM, and what did they say?** They'll probably reply that the PBM sets the rates, that higher pay costs taxpayers, or that you make money on other drugs. Do you know roughly what a fix would cost the plan? Is the $1.80 loss offset on brand-name or other drugs?

4. **How solid is the $1.80?** Is it based on invoices from all 38 pharmacies or from a sample? Is it an average across all 20 drugs? And about how many of your 3,100 plan prescriptions were those 20 generics? That tells me whether I can say what you personally lose in a year.

5. **Who is it addressed to, and who signs?** I need the plan director's name (or the board's), how the 38 will appear (all names, or a lead signer plus a list), and whether a state pharmacy association or anyone else is backing it.

6. **Is there one concrete local story you can use?** A county where your pharmacy is the only one, a patient who'd have to drive an hour, or one of the nine closures you know the reason for. Also, is there anything the plan or the papers already know that cuts against you? Examples would be past disputes, members of your group joining a PBM network voluntarily, or rates that went up somewhere else.

I've dropped the one-third claim and built the letter around what you can back up. It's about 430 words, so it fits on one page with the list of 38 pharmacies set in two or three columns underneath.

<final_document>
**An Open Letter to the [State Employees' Health Plan]**

To [Director's name] and the plan's board:

We are 38 independent pharmacies across [State]. Every week we fill prescriptions for state employees, retirees and their families who are covered by your plan. Your members account for about 22 percent of the prescriptions we fill, more than one in five.

Since January, your plan has paid us an average of $1.80 less per prescription than it costs us to buy and fill the 20 generic drugs we dispense most. We lose money on every one of those prescriptions. Some of us make back part of that loss on brand-name drugs. Not all of us do, and no pharmacy can run for long on the hope that one prescription will cover the loss on another.

This is already changing what we can offer your members. Two of our 38 pharmacies have told us they will stop filling prescriptions for plan members if the rates don't change. Nine independent pharmacies in [State] have closed in the past two years. We don't know how many of them closed because of rates, and we won't claim more than we know. We do know what happens to a town when its pharmacy stops serving the people who live there.

In 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most residents is an independent one, and the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away. If the pharmacy in one of those towns stops taking your plan, your members there face a round trip of more than 40 miles for their medicine, or a wait for it in the mail.

Your contract with your pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal on July 1. That is the time to fix this. We ask that the new contract pay pharmacies at least what each drug costs us to buy, plus a dispensing fee for filling it.

You don't have to take our word for the numbers. We will give your staff our purchase invoices for these 20 drugs so you can check them yourselves. We will also meet with your staff at any time before May 1 to go through them together.

Your members count on us, and we want to keep serving them. Please write the July 1 contract so that we can.

Sincerely,

Tom Reilly
Owner, Reilly Drug, Carver
On behalf of the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance
[Phone] · [Email]

**Member pharmacies of the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance**
[Pharmacy name, Town] × 38
</final_document>

Before it goes out:

- **Placeholders:** You'll need to fill in the plan's exact name, the director's name, the state and your contact details. The plan's website or annual report should list the director.
- **Check the $1.80 first.** You offered to share invoices, so the plan will take you up on it, and reporters may ask too. Find out whether the figure comes from all 38 pharmacies or a sample, and get the invoices together before you send.
- **Get consent from all 38 owners** to have their names on the list. Also confirm that the two who plan to stop filling are fine with being mentioned, even though the letter doesn't name them.
- **Ask whether anyone in the group has already contacted the plan or the PBM.** The letter doesn't mention past contact, but if someone did and the plan brings it up, you'll want to know.
